# Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

Your `r glossary("instruction file")` and skills are requests: nothing
guarantees that the model follows them. In this block you watch the controls
that do hold refuse something. You also find the route each one misses, so you
know what your repository prevents and what it only detects.

*⏱ ~25 minutes · Start on `main` (or `checkpoint-skills`), Git pane clean,
Claude Code running in Manual mode.*

:::{#block5-files .callout-note collapse="true"}

## Three kinds of guardrail

Beyond the instruction file, there are three kinds of guardrail. Each catches
what the others miss.

- **Permissions** decide what the agent may do without asking, and what it may
  never do. In Claude Code they live in `.claude/settings.json`: a starting
  mode (Manual asks before every edit and command) and deny rules. A deny rule
  *prevents*, but only on the routes it names.
- **Hooks** are your own code, which Claude Code runs at set moments: before a
  tool call, after an edit, before it stops. They suit "every time X happens,
  do Y". A hook that blocks by matching text is a tripwire, not a wall. The
  workshop ships none, on purpose: see *Do you need a hook?*, below.
- **Version tracking** lets you *detect* and *undo*. Git, through the Git pane,
  shows every change since your last commit, whatever made it, and reverts it.
  Claude Code's own undo, `/rewind`, is quicker but covers only changes made
  with its edit tools. Tests and checksums detect what should not have
  changed.

Prevent where you can, detect everything, and commit before the agent starts,
so that there is something to go back to.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How your workshop repository is guarded

Every guardrail below came with the template. You have been relying on them
since Block 2.

| Guardrail | Where it lives | Kind | Set up by |
|---|---|---|---|
| A git repository, clean before each task | `.git/`; the Git pane | Detect and undo | The template; you commit before each task |
| Manual mode | `.claude/settings.json` (`"defaultMode": "default"`) | Approval prompt | The template |
| 17 deny rules | `.claude/settings.json` | Prevent, on the routes they name | The template; you add one today |
| No command approved in advance | No `allow` list in the settings | Approval prompt | The template; `test_controls.R` checks it |
| Run `git status`; never touch raw data | `AGENTS.md` | Request | The template; yours since Block 4 |
| Tests, including `test_controls.R` | `tests/` | Detect | The template |
| Credentials kept out of commits | `.gitignore` lists `.Renviron` and `.env` | Prevent sharing | The template |
| A checksum of the raw data | `tests/test_cleaning.R` | Detect | The template; used in [Block 7](11g-data-cleaning.qmd) |
| Hooks | None | — | Not shipped: see *Do you need a hook?* |
| The sandbox | Not set | Prevent, by any route | Not available on native Windows ([Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd)) |
:::


## Exercise 1: What protects what?

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Match each asset to its guardrails (3 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** for each thing worth protecting, find what in your repository
prevents the damage and how you would notice it, so that you know which
guardrail you are relying on before an agent works near it.

Your instructor posts the table. Use *How your workshop repository is guarded*,
above, and answer in the Zoom chat, row by row: what prevents this here, and
if it went wrong anyway, how would you notice?

| Asset | What could go wrong | What prevents it here | How you would notice |
|---|---|---|---|
| `data/raw/` | Overwritten or "tidied" in place | | |
| `tests/fixtures/` | The reference regenerated by the code under test | | |
| `tests/` | A failing test edited until it passes | | |
| `.claude/`, `.posit/` | The agent's own guardrails switched off | | |
| `.Renviron`, `.env` | Credentials read and sent to the model provider | | |

The last two are easy to miss: the files that hold your controls are assets
too.

**You are done when** the group has an answer for both columns in every row.
Most "prevents" answers will be a deny rule; most "notice" answers will be "the
Git pane would show it" or "a test would fail".

::::
:::

Git detects only the changes since your last commit, so commit before an agent
starts. Some controls prevent and some only detect; Exercise 2 shows which.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The layers of control, and how each fails

| Layer | Example | What it does | How it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instruction | `AGENTS.md`, a skill | Requests | Silently ignored |
| Approval prompt | "Allow this command?" | Prevents, if you read it | Approval fatigue |
| Deny rule | `Edit(/data/raw/**)` | Prevents | Another route reaches the file |
| Hook | A script Claude Code runs before each tool call | Prevents | Rephrasing gets past it; by default, a crashing hook lets the call through |
| Sandbox | `/sandbox` (macOS, Linux, WSL2) | Prevents, by any route, for the paths you list | Not available on native Windows |
| Version control | The Git pane | Detects and undoes | Only changes since your last commit, and only if you look |
| Claude Code's undo | `/rewind` | Undoes | Only changes made with its edit tools, not R code it ran |
| Tests and checksums | testthat, `tools::md5sum()` | Detects | Only if they run |

Your repository's `AGENTS.md` asks the agent to run `git status` before it
edits anything, and to stop if there is no repository. That request helps, but
your commit is the control.
:::


## Exercise 2: Deny rules

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Read, test and add a rule, then find the gap (15 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** see a `r glossary("deny rule")` refuse, add one of your own and find
the route the rules do not cover, so that you know what your repository
prevents and what only git detects.

**Start state:** Git pane clean, Claude Code in Manual mode. Work on a scratch
file, never on real data.

**1. Make a scratch file and read the rules.** Run this in the R console:

```{r}
#| eval: false
writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

Commit it in the Git pane, so git can show any later change to it. In Claude
Code, type `/permissions` to list the 17 deny rules that your repository ships.

**2. See a rule refuse.**

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Add a second line, "test", to data/raw/scratch.csv.
```

"Denied by a permission rule" means the rule held, whatever the model
intended. The model may instead decline by itself, citing `AGENTS.md`. That was
a request that happened to work. To see the rule refuse, reply "This is a
scratch file; please make the edit with your edit tool".

**Answer each request with plain Yes or No.** Never choose an option that says
*don't ask again*: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. If
Claude Code asks to write the file another way, answer No: step 4 tries that.

**3. Add a rule yourself.** In `/permissions`, add
`Read(/data/confidential/**)`: habit 4 of the confidential-data habits in
[Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd), a speed bump rather than a
wall. When asked where to save it,
choose the project's shared settings file, `.claude/settings.json`, not the
local one (see *How it works*). It applies at once. You do not test this rule
here, because there is no `data/confidential/` folder. In your own project,
test it the way you test `Edit(/data/raw/**)` in this exercise.

**4. Find the gap.**

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Run this R code with Rscript: writeLines(c("a", "test"), "data/raw/scratch.csv")
```

Deny rules do not cover R code, so only the approval prompt stands in the way.
Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now;
refusing is always safe. Here you can: it writes to a scratch file, and you
want to see what catches the change. **Approve it.** The Git pane now shows the
file as modified, and **Diff** shows the new line: git caught what no rule
prevented.

Now try Claude Code's own undo. Type `/rewind` (or press Esc twice with the
prompt empty) and select your last prompt. The menu offers no *Restore code*:
`/rewind` restores only changes made with Claude Code's edit tools, and R code
changed this file. Choose *Never mind*. Only git can undo this change.

**5. Tidy up.** Undo the change with git: revert the file in the Git pane.
Then delete it, so that no scratch file is left among the raw data:

```{r}
#| eval: false
file.remove(here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

**6. Record, test and commit.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md`: ask the agent
to draft it, as in Block 3, then write the last part yourself. Note which
requests were refused, and what git caught and undid. Then
restart R (*Session → Restart R*) and run:

```{r}
#| eval: false
testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))
```

`test_controls.R` checks that Manual mode and every shipped rule are still in
place. It also checks that no command is approved in advance. `test_ai_log.R`
checks your new line. Commit the deletion of `scratch.csv`, your rule in
`.claude/settings.json` and the log line together.

**You are done when** you have seen a rule refuse, added one of your own, seen
the Git pane catch the R write that `/rewind` could not undo, `scratch.csv` is
gone, the test suite has no
failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your rule and log line are
committed.

**If it goes wrong:** if the model keeps declining in step 4, write the line
yourself in the console and carry on: the point is seeing git catch it. If
`/rewind` does offer *Restore code*, the agent changed some file with its edit
tool earlier in this conversation: choose *Never mind* anyway. If
"no command is approved in advance" fails, you chose *don't ask again*: remove
that allow rule in `/permissions`.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How it works: where the rules live

Your repository's `.claude/settings.json` starts the project in **Manual**
mode (`"defaultMode": "default"`: it asks before every edit and command). It
also holds 17 deny rules. They protect the raw data, the data provider's note,
the codebook, the checks, the references, the `r glossary("lockfile")` and the
settings themselves. You never need to edit the file: `/permissions` shows the
rules and adds new ones.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
#| class-output: json
cat(readLines(here::here("_instructor", "template-files", ".claude", "settings.json")), sep = "\n")
```

A leading `/` anchors a pattern to the project root. `Read` and `Edit` rules
cover Claude Code's own file tools, simple file commands it recognises (such as
`cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed` and `tee`) and shell redirects (`> file`). They do
not cover R code that it runs, or a command that never names the file, such as
a search of the whole project with `grep -r`. The documentation does not list
`rm`, `mv` or `cp`. The rules protect named files rather than whole folders, so the
agent can still write its scripts and tests in Blocks 7 and 8. `Edit(/renv.lock)` keeps
`renv::status()` a real check.

**Why the shared settings file.** `/permissions` can save a rule to
`.claude/settings.json`, which is committed with the project, or to the local
`.claude/settings.local.json`, which git ignores. Only a rule in the shared
file reaches a commit, and so reaches everyone who clones the repository.
Answering *don't ask again* saves an allow rule, usually in the local file.
That is why `test_controls.R` checks that no command is approved in advance.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using another tool

The exercises use Claude Code. **Posit Assistant** sets permissions per tool
in `.posit/assistant/settings.json` (for example `"bash": {"rm *": "deny"}`).
`deny` rules hold in every mode, including auto and YOLO. It has no documented
path rules for file edits, so rely on the Git pane in step 4 of Exercise 2. It
blocks reading `.env` and `.Renviron` by default.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Instructor: demonstration of a guard hook

A `r glossary("hook")` is a command that Claude Code itself (the
`r glossary("harness")`, not the model) runs before every
`r glossary("tool call")`. So it does not depend on the model following a
request. Your instructor saves the guard hook from *Going further* as
`hooks/guard_protected_paths.R` (the template does not ship `hooks/`). They
register it, run *Test the hook before you trust it* on the demonstration
machine, and repeat step 4. The hook, written in R, blocks any call that
mentions `data/raw`, so it blocks this one before any approval prompt. Then
they try the same write using `here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")`. The
text `data/raw` never appears, so the hook lets it through. A text-matching
hook is a tripwire, not a wall; the Git pane still shows the change. The GitHub
review gate (`r glossary("CODEOWNERS")`, `r glossary("branch protection")`) is
set up in the self-study page on
[GitHub Copilot's cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd).
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Do you need a hook?

The workshop ships no hooks. Before you add one to your own project, ask these
questions in order:

1. **Can a deny rule say it?** If the danger is a named file or a named
   command, use a rule: it needs no code and nothing to maintain.
2. **Must it hold whatever route the agent takes?** Then neither a rule nor a
   hook is enough. Keep the thing out of reach (outside the project, or behind
   the sandbox where it is available), and detect changes with git or a
   checksum.
3. **Is it "every time X happens, do Y"?** For example: run `lintr` or `styler`
   after each edit, run the tests before the agent says it is finished, notify
   you when it is waiting, or log every call. That is what hooks are for.
4. **Is it a judgement call?** For example, "prefer a mixed model when animals
   are measured twice". Then write an instruction or a skill
   ([Block 4](11e-instructions-skills.qmd)).

A hook has costs:

- **It is code.** It needs testing (*Test the hook before you trust it*, in
  *Going further*) and keeping up to date.
- **It runs on every matching call.** A hook written in R adds R's start-up
  time to each one.
- **It fails open by default.** If it crashes, the call goes ahead. From Claude
  Code v2.1.295, adding `"onFailure": "block"` to the hook makes a crash block
  the call instead.
- **It must match every route.** On Windows, Claude Code often runs commands
  through its PowerShell tool, so a hook that checks commands must match
  `PowerShell` as well as `Bash`.
- **It never approves anything.** A hook can only add a check: a call it lets
  through still faces your usual approval prompt.

**Ways to set one up:**

- Add a `hooks` block to `.claude/settings.json` yourself, as in *A guard hook*,
  in *Going further*.
- Ask Claude to draft the script and the settings for you, then read them and
  paste them in yourself. In the workshop repository, the deny rules keep it
  out of `.claude/` and `hooks/`.
- Set the environment variable `CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1` before you run
  `/init`. Claude Code then asks which of instruction files, skills and hooks
  to set up, explores the project, and shows you a proposal before it writes
  anything. Two cautions:
  - if you let it set up instruction files, it writes a `CLAUDE.md`, which
    hides an existing `AGENTS.md` ([Block 4](11e-instructions-skills.qmd));
  - once `Edit(/.claude/**)` is in place, its writes to the settings are
    refused, so run it before you add that rule.

To see which hooks are registered, type `/hooks`.
:::

:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** let an agent work in Manual mode in a repository where raw
  data, references and checks are protected, **trusted because** you have seen
  a deny rule refuse, seen git catch and undo the route it misses, and have a
  test that fails if the rules are weakened.
- **Check:** watch every control refuse something, and find the route it does
  not cover. What gets past the rules shows in the Git pane, Block 7's
  `r glossary("checksum")` test or `test_controls.R`.
- **Reproduce:** the rules live in `.claude/settings.json`, committed with the
  project, so everyone who clones it gets the same protection. Commit before
  each agent task: git can undo any change since then, and `/rewind` cannot
  undo what R code wrote.
- **Record:** your log line from step 6 notes which requests were refused and
  what git caught.
:::


## Set up guardrails in your own project

Your workshop repository came with its guardrails. A new project of your own
starts with none, so set them up before the agent's first task. This is not
covered live; it takes about 15 minutes.

1. **Version tracking first.** In the R console, run `usethis::use_git()`, then
   make a first commit. From then on, commit before every agent task. To undo,
   use `/rewind` for changes Claude made with its edit tools, and the Git pane
   for everything else.
2. **Permissions.** Download the starter `settings.json` below and save it as
   `.claude/settings.json`. Edit the paths to match your project. It starts in
   Manual mode and protects raw data, test references, the lockfile,
   credentials and itself. Add project-specific rules with `/permissions`.
3. **Instructions.** Copy the *Version control* section of your workshop
   `AGENTS.md` into your project's instruction file.
4. **Hooks, only if you need one.** Work through *Do you need a hook?*, above.
   If you will let `/init` set hooks up, run it before step 2, because
   `Edit(/.claude/**)` refuses its writes to the settings.
5. **Test it.** Ask the agent to edit a protected file, and watch the rule
   refuse. Copy `tests/test_controls.R` and change its list of rules to yours.
   Delete the tests for the `AGENTS.md` canary and `test_summary_functions.R`,
   unless your project has them. Then commit.

```{r}
#| echo: false
downloadthis::download_file(
  path = here::here("files", "controls", "settings.json"),
  output_name = "settings",
  output_extension = ".json",
  button_label = "Download the starter settings.json",
  button_type = "success",
  has_icon = TRUE,
  icon = "fa fa-save",
  self_contained = FALSE
)
```

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reference: the starter `settings.json`

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
#| class-output: json
cat(readLines(here::here("files", "controls", "settings.json")), sep = "\n")
```
:::

**Let Claude draft rules, never decide them.** You can ask it to propose deny
rules for a project, but read each one. A rule with a wrong path, such as a
missing leading `/`, protects nothing and fails silently. Claude Code asks
before every write to `.claude/`. The starter file's `Edit(/.claude/**)`
refuses such writes outright, so you install the rules yourself.

Protecting something new takes 30 seconds in `/permissions`. For confidential
data, add the five habits in [Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd).
Settings and hooks are code, so trust only repositories whose configuration
you have read.

  answer = "A checksum test or git status, because they inspect the file itself rather than the action that changed it",

))`

))`

:::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A guard hook

Claude Code itself, the harness rather than the model, runs a `PreToolUse`
hook before each tool call. It passes the hook the pending call as JSON on
standard input (stdin). If the hook exits with status 2, the call is denied
and its message is passed to the model. Exit status 0 does not approve the
call: it goes on to your usual approval prompt. Claude Code and Posit
Assistant use the same shape for this, so one script can serve both.

The guard below is written in R. It denies any edit, shell command or R code
that mentions a protected path.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# hooks/guard_protected_paths.R ----
# PreToolUse guard for Claude Code and Posit Assistant.
# Reads the pending tool call from stdin and exits 2 (deny) if the call
# mentions a protected path. A tripwire, not a wall: see "Break your own
# guard".

protected <- c(
  "data/raw",
  "tests/fixtures",
  "make_reference.R",
  ".github/workflows"
)

payload <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  paste(readLines(file("stdin"), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"),
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

# search the whole tool input as text, so the same rule covers file edits,
# shell commands and R code whatever the tool calls its fields
call_text <- as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(payload$tool_input, auto_unbox = TRUE))
hits <- protected[vapply(protected, \(p) grepl(p, call_text, fixed = TRUE), logical(1))]

if (length(hits) > 0) {
  message(
    "Blocked by project guard: this ", payload$tool_name,
    " call refers to a protected path (", paste(hits, collapse = ", "), "). ",
    "Do not modify protected files; ask the user to do it."
  )
  quit(save = "no", status = 2)
}

quit(save = "no", status = 0)
```

The template does not ship `hooks/`: save the script yourself as
`hooks/guard_protected_paths.R`, for example with
`usethis::edit_file("hooks/guard_protected_paths.R")`. It runs with
`Rscript --vanilla`, so it does not start renv. `jsonlite` must be installed in
your user library.

**Register it with Claude Code** by adding a `hooks` key to
`.claude/settings.json`, alongside the existing `permissions` key. The deny
rules protect `.claude/`, so make this edit yourself, not through the agent.

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|Bash|PowerShell",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "Rscript --vanilla \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/hooks/guard_protected_paths.R",
            "onFailure": "block"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The `matcher` lists the tool names the hook runs for. On Windows, Claude Code
often runs commands with its PowerShell tool rather than `Bash`, so a guard
that matches only `Bash` would never see them. `"onFailure": "block"` makes the
call fail if the hook itself crashes (Claude Code v2.1.295 or later; on older
versions, delete that line and rely on the test below). Type `/hooks` to check
that Claude Code has registered it.

**Register it with Posit Assistant** in `.posit/assistant/settings.json`. The
tool names differ: `edit`, `bash`, and `executeR` for R code run in your
session.

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "edit|bash|executeR",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Posit Assistant runs project hooks only in a workspace you have trusted.

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Test the hook before you trust it
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** check that the guard denies a protected path and allows a harmless
call, so that you know it works before you rely on it.

Hooks fail open by default. If the script crashes, for example because
`jsonlite` is not installed, both tools continue as if the hook had allowed the
call, unless you set `"onFailure": "block"` in Claude Code. Even then, a hook
that runs but checks the wrong thing allows everything. So test the script
directly, without the agent. The R below runs the hook exactly as Claude
Code does: as a fresh `Rscript --vanilla` process, given the tool call on
standard input. It works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
rscript <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript")
hook <- shQuote(here::here("hooks", "guard_protected_paths.R"))

run_hook <- function(json) {
  status <- system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", hook), input = json,
                    stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)
  status
}

# can the hook's own R session load jsonlite? 0 means yes
print(system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", "-e", shQuote("library(jsonlite)")),
              stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE))

# a call naming a protected path: expect 2
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript tests/make_reference.R"}}')

# a harmless call: expect 0
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript scripts/05_analysis.R"}}')
```

Any result other than 2 for the first call and 0 for the second means the hook
is broken and is silently allowing everything.

Now repeat the request from step 4 of Exercise 2. The R code mentions
`data/raw`, so the guard should deny it before you see an approval prompt.

To see exactly what each tool sends to hooks, add a temporary `PostToolUse`
hook with no matcher. Make it append its input to a log file, then read the
log. Posit Assistant's hooks documentation gives an example.

**You are done when** the protected call returns 2, the harmless call returns
0, and the request from step 4 of Exercise 2 is denied before you see an
approval prompt.

::::
:::
:::::

:::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Break your own guard

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Red-team the tripwire
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** get a write past the guard hook, so that you see where a
text-matching guard stops.

The live block removed the scratch file at the end. Recreate it first in the
R console, then commit it from the Git pane:

```{r}
#| eval: false
writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Run this R code:
writeLines(c("a", "test"), here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

The guard searches for the text `data/raw`. This call never contains it, because
`here::here()` assembles the path from separate pieces, so the guard allows the
call. A Windows path written with backslashes would also slip past.

This is the general limit of hooks that match text: they catch the obvious
form of a dangerous action, not every way of expressing it. Claude Code's
documentation makes the same point about command patterns. A guard hook is a
tripwire that stops accidents and makes intent visible; it is not a wall.
The Git pane still shows the change. Revert the file there, then delete it and
commit the deletion, as in steps 5 and 6 of Exercise 2.

**You are done when** the `here::here()` write has got past the guard, the Git
pane has shown the change, and you have deleted `scratch.csv` again.

::::
:::

**Why did `here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")` get past the guard
hook?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Hooks do not run for R code",
  answer = "The guard matches the text 'data/raw', and the call never contains that text",
  "here::here() runs with administrator rights",
  "The hook was registered for the wrong event"
))`

**Your guard hook depends on jsonlite, which is not installed, and you have
not set `onFailure`. What happens when the agent tries to edit a protected
file?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The edit is blocked, because the hook could not approve it",
  answer = "The edit goes ahead: hooks fail open by default, so a crashing hook is treated as allowing the call",
  "The agent stops and waits until jsonlite is installed",
  "The edit is blocked only in plan mode"
))`
:::::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The review gate on GitHub

Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely. There, the
controls are on the repository itself: CODEOWNERS, branch protection and a CI
check. The self-study page
[Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd)
sets them up.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Feedback hooks: useful, with a warning

Hooks can do more than block. A `PostToolUse` hook can run `lintr` on each R file
the agent edits and pass the result back to it. A `Stop` hook can run the test
suite and refuse to let the agent finish while tests fail. The second is
powerful and dangerous: an agent that is told it cannot stop until tests pass
may try to change the tests. Use it only when the deny rules and guard hook
protect `tests/`.
:::
